title: Sender Policy Framework (SPF) for Authorizing Use of Domains in Email, Version 1
summary: Email can be forged because existing protocols place no restriction on the MAIL FROM address or the HELO/EHLO domain a host uses. This document defines version 1 of the Sender Policy Framework, which lets domain owners say which hosts may send for them.

eli5.summary: Anyone can write any return address on an envelope. SPF lets a domain post a list of who is allowed to send as them.

questions: how does sender policy framework work
subtitle: How a domain publishes, in DNS, which servers may send its email, and how receivers check it.

tldr.problem: Email protocols let any sending host claim any domain in the MAIL FROM address or the HELO/EHLO greeting, which makes forging a domain easy and spam harder to fight.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes an SPF record, a DNS TXT record starting with v=spf1, listing the hosts allowed to use its name. A receiver runs the check_host() algorithm on the connecting IP address and gets one of seven results.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7208 obsoletes RFC 4408 and is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 7372, RFC 8553 and RFC 8616. SPF only authorizes the HELO and MAIL FROM identities, and the RFC sets no required action for any result.

today: RFC 7208 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 4408. It is updated by RFC 7372, RFC 8553 and RFC 8616, so it should be read together with them.

sections.title: The Forged Sender Problem
sections.content:
In Internet email, any host that injects mail can use any DNS domain name it wants in the identifiers defined by RFC 5321 and RFC 5322. That is convenient in some cases, but it is a major obstacle to reducing unsolicited bulk email, and the owners of a domain (an ADMD, or ADministrative Management Domain) are rightly worried about others using their name.

The Sender Policy Framework (SPF) lets an ADMD authorize which hosts may use its domain name in two identities: MAIL FROM (the envelope sender) and HELO (the name an SMTP client gives in HELO or EHLO). Compliant domains publish SPF records in DNS, and compliant receivers use those records to test the sending MTA.

There is a second benefit for receivers. Once an identity is verified, local policy can be based on the sender's domain rather than the host's IP address, and the RFC argues that the reputation of a domain is likely to be more accurate because domains are more stable over time. If the claimed identity fails, policy can take stronger action such as rejecting the mail.
sections.eli5: Anyone can write any return address on an envelope. SPF is a guest list the real address owner posts, so the mail room can tell if a sender is on it.

sections.title: SPF Records in DNS
sections.content:
An SPF record is one string in a single DNS TXT record (type 16) at the domain name it describes, not in a subdomain. SPF records MUST be published as TXT only. The old dedicated SPF record type (code 99) was dropped, because the working group concluded that migrating to it was very unlikely. A domain MUST NOT have multiple records that would make a check select more than one.

A record starts with the version v=spf1, followed by space-separated terms. An example is v=spf1 +mx a:colo.example.com/28 -all, which has three directives. A directive is an optional qualifier followed by a mechanism: + (pass, the default), a minus sign (fail), ~ (softfail) or ? (neutral).

Size matters. A record may be split into several quoted strings, which are joined without spaces, to get around the 255-octet limit on one string. The RFC says a record SHOULD stay small enough that the DNS answer fits within 512 octets, with a guideline of 450 octets for the whole DNS message, because oversized records could be silently ignored by verifiers. Wildcard records are discouraged, and a wildcard needs the record repeated for every name that has other records and for the subdomains below it.
sections.eli5: The guest list is written on a card pinned to the domain's door in the phone book of the Internet. It starts with a version number and then lists rules, one after another.

sections.title: Checking and the Seven Results
sections.content:
A receiver, usually the receiving MTA, runs the check during the SMTP transaction, at the time of the MAIL command, using the MAIL FROM value and the client IP address. Doing it later can make legitimate mail fail because the sender's policy has changed, and it is harder to extract the right data from deceptive headers. Rejecting after acceptance also produces backscatter, which the RFC tells operators to avoid.

The RFC recommends checking the HELO identity first and then MAIL FROM. A HELO record refers to a single host, so it is a reliable signal, and a conclusive HELO result saves the cost of the more complex MAIL FROM check. MAIL FROM MUST be checked if HELO was not checked or did not give a definitive result. When the reverse-path is null, as for bounces, MAIL FROM is taken to be postmaster at the HELO name. Checking other identities without the publisher's explicit approval is NOT RECOMMENDED.

The outcome is one of seven results: none, neutral, pass, fail, softfail, temperror and permerror. The protocol itself sets no normative requirement for what to do with any of them; that is local policy.
sections.eli5: When a letter arrives, the mail room looks at the sender's guest list right away, while the delivery truck is still at the door, and writes down one of seven answers.

sections.title: The check_host() Algorithm
sections.content:
The function check_host() takes the client IP address, a domain, and the sender identity, and returns a result. Implementations may use another algorithm so long as results are always the same. It first returns none if the domain is malformed, is not a multi-label name, or the lookup gives NXDOMAIN. A server failure or timeout gives temperror.

It then queries TXT records and discards any that do not begin with exactly v=spf1, so v=spf10 does not match. No remaining record gives none, and more than one gives permerror. Any syntax error anywhere in the chosen record also gives permerror, before any evaluation.

Terms are evaluated left to right. The first mechanism that matches decides the result through its qualifier. If none match and there is no redirect, the result is neutral, as if ?all were at the end. The RFC advises ending a record with all or redirect to make that explicit.

To limit DNS load, implementations MUST allow at most 10 terms that cause DNS queries (include, a, mx, ptr, exists and redirect) and return permerror beyond that. An mx evaluation MUST NOT query more than 10 address records. Implementations SHOULD also limit void lookups (queries with an empty answer or NXDOMAIN) to two, and SHOULD allow at least 20 seconds overall, returning temperror if time runs out.
sections.eli5: The mail room reads the rules one by one and stops at the first one that fits. It also refuses to chase more than ten leads, so a trick list cannot keep it busy forever.

sections.title: Mechanisms and Modifiers
sections.content:
A mechanism tests whether the client IP address is covered. all always matches and is used last. ip4 and ip6 compare against a network, with a default prefix of /32 and /128. a matches the address records of a name (and AAAA for IPv6), and mx matches the addresses of the domain's MX hosts. For mx, a missing MX record MUST NOT fall back to the implicit MX rule of RFC 5321. exists does an A lookup on a built name and matches if any record comes back, which allows very fine-grained rules.

include:domain runs check_host() recursively on another domain. Only the evaluated result is used: a pass there makes the include match, while fail, softfail and neutral do not match. The RFC admits the name was poorly chosen, since a -all in the included record does not end the outer evaluation. It is meant for crossing administrative boundaries.

ptr uses reverse DNS and SHOULD NOT be published. The RFC calls it slow, less reliable and a burden on .arpa servers, though implementations MUST still support it.

A modifier carries extra information after an equals sign. redirect=domain applies the other domain's record when nothing matched, and lets one record serve many domains inside one ADMD. It is ignored if the record has an all. exp=domain names a TXT record whose text, macro-expanded, explains a fail. Each of the two MUST NOT appear more than once, and unknown modifiers MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: The guest list can say: this exact address is okay, any house on this street is okay, or go check that other list. It can also say: if nothing matches, use the same list as my sister.

sections.title: Macros
sections.content:
Macros let a record contain placeholders that are filled in with details of the current message and connection. They are written %{letter}. Common letters are s (the sender), l (its local part), o (its domain), d (the domain being checked), i (the client IP address), v (in-addr or ip6) and h (the HELO name). The letters c, r and t work only in exp text. The p letter exists but SHOULD NOT be published.

Optional transformers change the value. A number keeps that many right-hand parts, r reverses the parts, and delimiters other than the dot can be given for splitting. The RFC example is a client of 192.0.2.1: %{i} gives 192.0.2.1 and %{ir} gives 1.2.0.192. A capital letter is URL-escaped. A % not followed by {, %, hyphen or underscore is a syntax error giving permerror.

Macros cost caching efficiency. If no processed directive used s, l, o or h, results can be cached on domain and IP address alone until the shortest TTL expires. Senders should avoid those macros in mechanisms when they can. Expanded names longer than 253 characters are truncated from the left, by whole labels.
sections.eli5: A macro is a blank in a form, like Dear ___. The mail room fills in the blank with the real address of the letter in front of it.

sections.title: Handling Results and Deploying SPF
sections.content:
Receivers are free to choose what each result means. Treat neutral exactly like none, so that domains are not discouraged from testing SPF. softfail sits between fail and neutral: receivers SHOULD NOT reject solely on it. For fail, local policy applies, and a rejecting receiver SHOULD use SMTP reply 550 with enhanced code 5.7.1. For temperror the suggested reply is 451 with 4.4.3, and for permerror it is 550 with 5.5.2. Receivers that do not reject SHOULD add a Received-SPF or Authentication-Results header so later software can see the result.

For publishers, cheaper mechanisms should come first. The RFC ranks ip4 entries as the best record, and calls a record that depends on a wide mx expensive. It also gives standard advice: a domain that sends no mail should publish v=spf1 -all, and a mail host should publish v=spf1 a -all for its own name. Because the HELO name is the only identity in a null-sender bounce, it needs a correct SPF record too.

Mailing lists and other mediators are a known trouble spot. SPF checks the IP address of the last server, so if a mediator keeps the original MAIL FROM, a check against the original domain will fail unless mitigations are used.
sections.eli5: The rules say what the answers mean, but each mail room decides what to do. A mailing list that re-sends your letter can look like a stranger using your return address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Much of this section is about denial of service. A hostile record can make verifiers query a victim: for example, an attacker can publish an a mechanism list pointing at the victim and send mail in volume to many receivers, who then do the lookups. That is why the processing limits must be low, and why the RFC recommends aborting with permerror after more than two void lookups.

SPF has narrow reach. Passing only authorizes the MAIL FROM and HELO identities, and a message can still show other identities, such as the From: header, that look different. It also cannot tell users of the same MTA apart, so cross-user forgery has to be prevented by the mail service, for example with SMTP AUTH. The check relies on DNS, so spoofed DNS data could produce wrong results, and the RFC points to DNSSEC as a countermeasure.

Other points: explanation strings come from the sender's domain and can contain malicious URLs or misleading text. Macros let senders put arbitrary text into receiver DNS queries. SPF queries, especially from exists, can reveal who is sending mail and to which MTA. Delivering mail that gets fail admits content explicitly not authorized by the purported sender.
sections.eli5: Bad people could write a list that sends the mail room on a wild goose chase. So the mail room has strict limits, and it also remembers the list only covers the return address, not everything written on the letter.

items.label: None
items.desc: No valid domain could be extracted, or no SPF record was found.

items.label: Neutral
items.desc: The domain explicitly makes no statement about this client.

items.label: Pass
items.desc: The client is authorized to send with this identity.

items.label: Fail
items.desc: The client is explicitly not authorized.

items.label: Softfail
items.desc: Weak statement that the host is probably not authorized.

items.label: Temperror
items.desc: A transient (generally DNS) error. A retry may succeed.

items.label: Permerror
items.desc: The published records could not be interpreted; needs the DNS operator.
